title: TPO1-based polyamines transport contributes to pathogenicity of sugarcane smut fungus

sections.abstract:
The basidiomycete Sporisorium scitamineum causes sugarcane smut disease, leading to a significant impairment in the quality and yield of sugarcane. Polyamines affect the intracellular redox balance, which is important for the pathogenic development of S. scitamineum , including sexual mating, dikaryotic hyphae growth, and host invasion. In the present study, we identified a polyamine transporter, SsTPO1, in S. scitamineum . Deletion or overexpression of SsTPO1 led to the disruption of intracellular levels of putrescine, spermidine, and spermine in opposite directions. SsTPO1-based polyamine homeostasis contributes to dikaryotic hyphal growth and host invasion after sexual mating, likely by affecting the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway and collaboratively regulating redox homeostasis. Environmental pH affected SsTPO1-mediated polyamine transport, so S. scitamineum hyphae growth favoured neutral to alkaline environments rather than acidic conditions. The SsTPO1-based polyamine transport also participates in stress resistance and autophagy induction. In summary, our work revealed that SsTPO1 facilitates polyamine transport to regulate cell growth, differentiation, and fungal pathogenicity in S. scitamineum .

KEYWORDS: Polyamines, MFS transporters, sexual mating/filamentation, pathogenicity, Sporisorium scitamineum
sections.introduction:
Polyamines are biologically active aliphatic nitrogen-containing bases involved in cell growth and development, and their levels are tightly controlled through biosynthesis, oxidation, acetylation, degradation, and transport (Igarashi and Kashiwagi 2000 ). The transport of polyamines is vital for maintaining homeostasis, encompassing both the absorption and secretion processes. Several systems for polyamine absorption and secretion have been identified in bacteria, with Escherichia coli being among the most extensively studied. Bacterial transport systems include the ABC transport system and bidirectional and unidirectional transporters (Kurihara and Suzuki 2015 ). Furthermore, the APC (amino acid-polyamine-organocation) superfamily plays a crucial role in polyamine efflux, significantly contributing to the dynamic balance of polyamines within bacterial cells (Jack et al. 2000 ).

Polyamine transporters have been reported in yeast and filamentous fungi (Davis and Ristow 1988 ; Hoyt and Davis 2004 ). Saccharomyces cerevisiae TPO1-TPO5 belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) and are specifically involved in polyamine transport (Tomitori et al. 1999 ; Tomitori et al. 2001 ; Albertsen et al. 2003 ; Tachihara et al. 2005 ). Environmental pH plays a crucial role in TPO1-mediated polyamine transport, as TPO1 mediates polyamine secretion in acidic environments and polyamine uptake in alkaline environments (Uemura et al. 2005 ; Sampathkumar and Drouin 2015 ). Transcriptional regulation of the TPO (Polyamine transporter) genes is responsible for spermidine (SPD)-induced oxidative stress in yeast (Teixeira et al. 2011 ). In Aspergillus fumigatus , TPO3 and DUR3 maintain polyamine homeostasis, which in turn modulates reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and susceptibility to the antifungal drug itraconazole (ITC) (Chen et al. 2020 ). Despite the importance of polyamine transporters in various fungal species, they have not yet been investigated in S. scitamineum .

Our previous research elucidated the significance of polyamine biosynthesis and oxidation in S. scitamineum (Yin et al. 2024a , 2024b ). Here, we identified a polyamine transporter orthologous to S. cerevisiae TPO1, and thus named it SsTPO1, which mediates polyamine transport in a pH-dependent manner. Notably, SsTPO1 is important for sporidia growth, dikaryotic hyphae growth after sexual mating, and invasive growth during the early stage of host infection in S. scitamineum . Furthermore, SsTPO1-based polyamine transport crosstalk with the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway regulates oxidative stress resistance and autophagy induction. In conclusion, our study revealed that SsTPO1 facilitates polyamine transport to maintain intracellular polyamine homeostasis, which is favourable for the formation and invasive growth of pathogenic hyphae in S. scitamineum .
sections.methods:
Wild-type strains of opposite mating types, MAT-1 and MAT-2 (Yan et al. 2016 ), were used for generating the mutants in this study, as listed in Table S1.

To induce sexual mating, fresh haploid sporidia were cultured overnight in liquid Yeast Extraction-Peptone-Sucrose (YePS; comprising 1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, and 2% sugar, pH 6.5) medium, washed twice with sterilised ddH 2 O, and adjusted to OD 600 = 1.0. Equal volumes of haploid sporidia from opposite mating types were mixed and spotted onto solid PDA (prepared with 4% PDA powder, sourced from DingGuo, Guangzhou, China) or minimal medium (MM; consisting of 0.17% yeast nitrogen base, 2% glucose, and 10 mmol/L ammonium sulfate, pH 6.8). The cultures were incubated in the dark at 28 °C for 2−3 d and then photographed.

To assess growth of the haploid sporidia, freshly cultured haploid sporidia (adjusted to OD 600 = 1.0) were serially diluted to CFU = 10 7 , 10 6 , 10 5 , 10 4 , and 10 3 , respectively, spotted onto PDA or MM medium, and incubated in the dark at 28 °C for 2−3 d before photographing.

For growth curve analysis, YePS-cultured haploid sporidia (adjusted to OD 600 = 0.01) were allowed to grow in a 100-well honeycomb plate in an automatic microbial growth curve analyzer (Oy Growth Curves Ab Ltd.; Bioscreen C) at 28 °C for 3 d. OD 600 values were recorded at 60 min intervals.

For autophagy induction, the sporidia of the tested strains were liquid-cultured in YePS at 28 °C for 16 h, then washed with sterilised ddH 2 O, and transferred to nitrogen depletion conditions (cultured in MM-N for 4 h) to induce non-selective autophagy.

Pathogenicity analysis follows the established protocol (Gan et al. 2022 ) with minor modification, to ensure successful infection by the fungal pathogen. The stem sections of sugarcane (ROC22 cultivar) were soaked in 1 L of spore suspension (v:v = 1:1) of either MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE for 30 min. The treated sections were then planted in pots, with 5–6 sections per pot. After 2–3 weeks, 1 mL of spore suspension (v:v = 1:1) of MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE was injected into the sugarcane seedlings, with sterile ddH 2 O injection serving as a blank control.

Putrescine (Sigma-Aldrich, United States, 51799), spermidine trihydrochloride (Sigma-Aldrich, S2501), spermine (Sigma-Aldrich, S3256), adenosine 3’,5’-cyclic monophosphate (3’,5’-cAMP, Sigma-Aldrich, 60-92-4), H 2 O 2 (DaMao, China), N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC, Aladdin, 619-91-1), GSH (Glutathione Reduced, Aladdin, 70-18-8), VC (Vitamin C, Aladdin, 50-81-7), and RAPA (Rapamycin, Aladdin, 53123-88-9).

To verify the ss1tpo1 Δ and ss2tpo1 Δ mutants, 5 μg of genomic DNA was extracted from the respective strains using the Fungal DNA Midi Kit (Omega, D3590-01). Genomic DNA was digested with Pvu I (NEB, R3150V)/ BamH I (NEB, R0136V) and separated by electrophoresis on a 0.75% agarose gel. The separated DNA fragments were transferred from agarose gel to a Hybond-N + membrane (Amersham, RPN203B). For probe labelling, targeted fragment hybridisation, and detection in Southern blot analysis, a digoxigenin (DIG) High Prime DNA labeling and detection starter kit II (Roche, Mannheim, Germany) was used, following the protocols provided by the manufacturer.

Total RNA was extracted using the FastPure Plant Total RNA Isolation Kit (Vazyme, RC401-01). cDNA was synthesised using a HiScript® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (+gDNA wiper; Vazyme, R312-01). RT-qPCR was performed on a QuantStudio™ 6 Flex (Life Technologies, USA) using ChamQ™ Universal SYBR® qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q311-02). Relative gene expression was calculated using the ΔΔCt method (Livak and Schmittgen 2001 ), with fungal ACTIN or the sugarcane glyceraldehyde dehydrogenase ( GAPDH ) gene serving as an internal control. All experiments were conducted with three independent biological repeats, each containing three technical replicates.

DNA fragments were constructed upstream and downstream (each approximately 1 kb) of the target gene fracking the selection marker, hygromycin resistance gene HPT or Zeocin resistance gene ZEO , by double-joint PCR amplification (Yu et al. 2004 ). To generate SsTPO1 overexpression strains, a reintegrated homologous fragment, composed of the upstream fragment of LB -SsTPO1 , a strong and constitutive promoter P GAPD , coding sequence of mCherry and SsTPO1 , expression cassette of ZEO R gene, and the downstream fragment of SsTPO1- RB, was amplified by fusion PCR. To generate the GFP-SsATG8:MAT-1 strain, a reintegrated homologous fragment, composed of the native promoter of SsATG8 (LB -SsATG8 ), coding sequence of GFP and SsATG8 , expression cassette of ZEO R gene, and the downstream fragment of SsATG8- RB, was amplified by fusion PCR. All hygromycin-resistant or zeocin-resistant transformants were first screened by PCR or RT-qPCR and then confirmed by Southern blot analysis or fluorescence detection. The primers used for constructing the deletion, overexpression, or tagging fragments, or for verification of fungal transformants, are listed in Table S2.

The constructed DNA fragments used for gene deletion, overexpression, or tagging were introduced into fungal cells via polyethylene glycol (PEG)-mediated protoplast transformation following established protocols (Yin et al. 2024a ).

An Axio Observer Z1 microscope (Zeiss, Jena, Germany) equipped with an sCMOS camera (PCO Edge, Kelheim, Germany) was employed to observe and capture images of 3,3’-diaminobenzidine (DAB, Macklin)-stained sugarcane tissues infected by S. scitamineum . A confocal microscope (Leica, STELLARIS 5, Germany) equipped with a HC PL APO CS2 63x/1.40 oil immersion objective was employed to observe and capture images of the GFP or mCherry signals, with 488 nm excitation and 500−535 nm emission, and with 561 nm excitation and 570−620 nm emission wavelengths respectively.

Three-dimensional structure of SsTPO1 protein ( CDR88715.1 ) was downloaded from AlphaFold Protein Structure Database ( https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/A0A0F7S1B5 ), and three-dimensional structures of polyamines (PUT, SPD, SPM, respectively) from PubChem ( https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ ). Molecular docking analysis of SsTPO1 with polyamines was performed using SwissDock ( https://www.swissdock.ch/ ) powered by AutoDock Vina (Eberhardt et al. 2021 ), and visualised using PyMOL software (version 3.0).

Polyamine extraction and detection followed the established methods (Yin et al. 2024a ). Intracellular H 2 O 2 was extracted and quantified using an Amplex™ Red Hydrogen Peroxide/Peroxidase Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher, A22188) with minor modifications to the manufacturer’s instructions (Yin et al. 2024a ). Intracellular cAMP was extracted and quantified using a complete cAMP ELISA Kit (Catalog #: ADI-900-163A).

Total protein extracts were fractionated by SDS-PAGE (SurePAGE™, Bis-Tris, 15%) and then transferred to a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane. Anti-ATG8 antibody (MBL, PM090) was used as the primary antibody. HRP and Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (Abbkine, A21020) were used as the secondary antibodies. An Efficient Chemiluminescence kit (Genview, GE2301-50 ML) was used for signal detection. The pixel intensity of the detected protein bands was determined using ImageJ software (version 1.53 k).

Statistical analysis was performed with GraphPad Prism 7 software, using the Multiple t test method.
sections.results:
We used the sequence of the pH-mediated polyamine transporter TPO1 in S. cerevisiae (Tomitori et al. 1999 ) (accession number: NP_013072.1 ) as a query to search for an ortholog in S. scitamineum by using the BLASTP website ( https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi?PROGRAM=blastp&PAGE_TYPE=BlastSearch&LINK_LOC=blasthome ). A total of 25 proteins were identified. Domain comparison among these proteins revealed that they belong to the MFS superfamily, characterised by either the MFS_Tpo1_MDR_like domain or the MFS superfamily domain (Figure S1A). Furthermore, we conducted a phylogenetic analysis of the TPO orthologs from S. scitamineum in comparison with S. cerevisiae TPO1-TPO5. We noticed that two S. scitamineum TPO orthologs clustered with S. cerevisiae TPO5, six clustered with TPO2 and TPO3, and ten clustered with TPO1 and TPO4 (Figure S1B). The protein with accession number CDR88715.1 is among the proteins clustered in S. cerevisiae TPO1 and TPO4 groups, and we named it SsTPO1. Using the DeepTMHMM tool ( https://dtu.biolib.com/DeepTMHMM ), 12 membrane-spanning regions were predicted in SsTPO1, with a topology of N - and C-termini inside the cell (Figure S1C). Molecular docking results indicated that SsTPO1 could bind to polyamines (Figure S2A).

We then generated deletion mutants of SsTPO1 gene (accession number SPSC_05547 ) in both MAT-1 and MAT-2 backgrounds, and verified the transformants by Southern blotting (Figure S2B). Single-deletion mutants in the MAT-1 and MAT-2 backgrounds were designated as ss1tpo1 Δ and ss2tpo1 Δ, respectively. Concurrently, we created overexpression strains, named Ss1TPO1-OE and Ss2TPO1-OE , as confirmed by RT-qPCR (Figure S2C).

To investigate the role of SsTPO1 in polyamine transport, we measured the intracellular levels of PUT, SPD, and SPM in wild-type ( MAT-1 ), ss1tpo1 Δ, Ss1TPO1-OE , MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE . The results showed that the intracellular PUT levels in ss1tpo1 Δ were lower than those in MAT-1 ( p < 0.0001), whereas the intracellular SPD ( p < 0.0001) and SPM ( p < 0.05) levels were higher than those in MAT-1 . In contrast, intracellular SPD ( p < 0.01) and SPM ( p < 0.05) levels were slightly lower in Ss1TPO1-OE than in MAT-1 ( Figure 1A ). Under sexual mating/filamentation conditions, SPD levels in Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE was lower than those in MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( p < 0.001), while SPD levels in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ was higher than those in MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( p < 0.0001), whereas PUT levels were much higher in Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE than in MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( p < 0.0001) ( Figure 1B ). To further verify the role of SsTPO1 in polyamine transport, we overexpressed the SsTPO1 gene in the ss1samdc Δ strain that was reported defective in PUT to SPD conversion (Yin et al. 2024a ). Two independent GAPD:SsTPO1 ( ss1samdc Δ) strains were cultured in liquid YePS medium to test their auxotrophy for SPD. Indeed, GAPD:SsTPO1 ( ss1samdc Δ) strains could not grow in YePS medium, while supplementation with SPD (1 mmol/L) could completely restore growth of these two strains ( Figure 1C ). Similar results were obtained for the strains grown on solid medium (Figure S3A). These results indicate that SsTPO1 is likely to mediate the uptake of PUT and efflux of SPD and SPM under neutral pH culture conditions.

SsTPO1-based polyamines transport regulates dikaryotic hyphae growth. (A, B) Measurement of intracellular polyamines. (C) Growth assay of the indicated strains, in YePS medium at 28 °C for 2 d containing or without (control) SPD (1 mmol/L). (D) Mating assay of the indicated strains, grown on PDA containing or without (control) PUT, SPD, or SPM (0.1 mmol/L or 1 mmol/L). MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). Scale bar = 1 mm. (E) Transcriptional profiling of genes controlling sexual mating and hyphae growth by RT-qPCR, and the relative fold changes were calculated using the -ΔΔCt method (Livak and Schmittgen 2001 ). 50 μL of sporidia ( OD 600 = 1.0) of opposite mating-types were mixed and inoculated on solid YePS medium, and allowed to grow at 28 °C for 2 d, before total RNA extraction. ACTIN gene served as an internal control. For the bar charts in (A), (B), and (E), mean ± S.E. was derived from three independent biological repeats, each containing three replications ( n = 3). *, **, ***, ****, p < 0.05, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001, respectively, vs. wild type ( MAT-1 or MAT-1 × MAT-2 ) (Student’s T test). ns: No significance.

Overall, we identified a candidate TPO1 protein named SsTPO1 that facilitates polyamine transport in S. scitamineum .

To investigate the biological role of SsTPO1 , we assessed sporidia growth in MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE strains under various conditions. Exogenous PUT, SPD, or SPM (0.1 mmol/L or 1 mmol/L) was supplemented to investigate the effects of polyamines on sporidia growth on solid MM or PDA. The results showed that, under all treatment conditions, the ss1tpo1 Δ mutant exhibited stronger growth than MAT-1 , whereas the Ss1TPO1-OE strains exhibited weaker growth than MAT-1 (Figure S3B). Microscopic analysis revealed that the morphology of the Ss1TPO1-OE strain was different from that of MAT-1 and ss1tpo1 Δ mutants (Figure S3C). Subsequently, we examined the growth curves of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE sporidia cultured in liquid medium, and found no significant difference between MAT-1 and ss1tpo1 Δ strains, but the logarithmic growth phase of the Ss1TPO1-OE strain was significantly delayed compared to that of MAT-1 (Figure S3D). We concluded that SsTPO1 is important for sporidia growth in S. scitamineum .

Furthermore, we evaluated the growth of dikaryotic hyphae (after sexual mating) of MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE on solid MM or PDA media. Our results showed that when cultured on a solid MM medium, dikaryotic hyphae were barely formed in MAT-1 × MAT-2 and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE , whereas distinct dikaryotic hyphae were formed in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ (Figure S3E). The hyphal growth of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ was significantly enhanced compared to MAT-1 × MAT-2 on PDA medium ( Figure 1D ). Moreover, the dikaryotic hyphae in Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE were significantly shorter than those in MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( Figure 1D ). To further elucidate the role of polyamines in dikaryotic hyphae growth, we added exogenous PUT, SPD, and SPM (0.1 or 1 mmol/L) to solid MM or PDA media. Our results showed that on solid MM medium, the addition of exogenous PUT (1 mmol/L) slightly inhibited the dikaryotic hyphae of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, but had no effect on the MAT-1 × MAT-2 or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE (Figure S3E). SPD (1 mmol/L) slightly promoted dikaryotic hyphae in all mating strains (Figure S3E). On PDA medium, PUT (1 mmol/L) slightly inhibited dikaryotic hyphae in MAT-1 × MAT-2 . SPD (1 mmol/L) slightly promoted dikaryotic hyphae formation in MAT-1 × MAT-2 and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( Figure 1D ). In particular, SPM (0.1 mmol/L) significantly inhibited dikaryotic hyphae in MAT-1 × MAT-2 and ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, but did not affect the overexpression of Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( Figure 1D ). SPM (1 mmol/L) completely inhibited dikaryotic hyphae in MAT-1 × MAT-2 and ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, but Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE still produced very short dikaryotic hyphae ( Figure 1D ).

RT-qPCR analysis revealed that the sexual mating genes ( SsGPA3 , SsUAC1 , and SsADR1 in the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway; SsFUZ7 , SsKPP4 , and SsKPP2 in the MAPK signaling pathway; SsbE and SsbW in the b locus controlling filamentous growth; SsCRK1 encoding a protein kinase controlling sexual mating) were significantly down-regulated in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, whereas SsPRF1 (encoding the master transcriptional factor controlling mating/filamentous growth) was up-regulated for more than 20-folds, compared to MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( Figure 1E ), which may explain the enhanced dikaryotic hyphae in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ. Similarly, SsGPA3 , SsUAC1 , SsADR1 , SsFUZ7 , SsKPP4 , SsKPP2 , SsPRF1 , SsROP1 , and SsCRK1 were significantly down-regulated in Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE compared to MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( Figure 1E ).

In conclusion, SsTPO1-mediated polyamine transport is required for sporidia growth and negatively regulates dikaryotic hyphal growth in S. scitamineum .

We further evaluated the role of SsTPO1 in S. scitamineum pathogenicity. Typical smut disease symptoms appeared in sugarcane 3–6 months after infection ( Figure 2A ). The disease rate for MAT-1 × MAT-2 infected sugarcane ( n = 15) was 38.75% ± 1.25%, and 7.5% ± 7.5% for ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ infection ( n = 15) ( Figure 2B ). In contrast, similar to the blank control, sugarcane plants ( n = 15) inoculated with the Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE mutant did not exhibit any disease symptoms, specifically smut whip formation ( Figure 2A,B ).

SsTPO1 is required for Sporisorium scitamineum pathogenicity. (A) 1 mL mixed sporidia of the indicated strains were used for soaking of the sugarcane stem sections before planting, and for injection into the sugarcane seedlings. ddH 2 O served as a blank control. Each treatment contained at least 15 seedlings ( n ≥ 15). The ‘black whip’ symptoms in the red box were enlarged. (B) Incidence rate. (C) Quantitative analysis of the height of infected seedlings. n = 21, 22, 15, and 15, respectively. (D) Microscopic images of the infected sugarcane plant tissues. White arrows: teliospores and fungal mycelia. Scale bar = 50 μm. (E) Transcriptional profiling of the plant-pathogen interaction-related genes in sugarcane seedlings at 96 hpi compared to 48 hpi following S. scitamineum infection. Sugarcane GAPDH gene served as an internal control. (F) Quantitative analysis of fungal biomass by qPCR. The infected stems (about 3 cm) were sampled for DNA extraction at 3 and 7 dpi. Fungal ACTIN gene and sugarcane GAPDH gene served as internal controls. For the bar charts in (B), (C), (E), and (F), mean ± S.E. was derived from three independent biological repeats, each containing three replications. MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). For (B) and (C), *, p < 0.05, **, p < 0.01, ns represents no significance, vs. MAT-1 × MAT-2 . For (E), different letters denote significant difference ( p < 0.05). For (F), **, p < 0.01, vs. WT (7 dpi), ns represents no significance.

The average height of the sugarcane plants was measured as an indicator of smut infection. We found that sugarcane plants inoculated with the overexpression strains were significantly taller than those inoculated with the wild-type or deletion strains ( Figure 2C ). Following disease incidence and sugarcane height assessment, we collected apical plant tissues from the sugarcane seedlings for microscopic examination. We found abundant brown-black teliospores and hyphae ( Figure 2D , white arrows) in tissues inoculated with MAT-1 × MAT-2 , whereas only hyphae ( Figure 2D , white arrows) were observed in tissues inoculated with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE .

To further investigate the potential role of SsTPO1 in the early infection stages, we assessed the relative expression levels of plant-pathogen interaction-related genes and fungal biomass in sugarcane seedlings using RT-qPCR. The relative expression levels of LRR-RLK (leucine-rich repeat receptor-like protein kinase), MAPK , and WRKY5 (WRKY transcription factor 5) were significantly lower at 48 and 96 hpi following infection with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE compared to MAT-1 × MAT-2 , while MEK (mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase) showed no significant change ( Figure 2E ). In contrast, fungal biomass was lower in plants infected with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE than in those infected with MAT-1 × MAT-2 at 7 days post-infection (dpi) ( Figure 2F ).

In conclusion, SsTPO1 is crucial for early host colonisation and is therefore required for S. scitamineum pathogenicity.

Next, we evaluated whether SsTPO1 was involved in the stress resistance of S. scitamineum . Sporidia of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE strains were allowed to grow under osmotic (500 mmol/L NaCl; 1 mol/L sorbitol) or cell wall stress (0.5 mmol/L Congo red, CR; 0.1 mmol/L SDS) conditions. The ss1tpo1 Δ mutant exhibited higher tolerance to osmotic stress or cell wall stress than MAT-1 did, whereas the Ss1TPO1-OE strain was hypersensitive to these stressful conditions (Figure S4A). ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ displayed a higher tolerance to SDS (0.1 mmol/L, cell wall stress) than MAT-1 × MAT-2 , which in turn was more tolerant than Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE (Figure S4B). MAT-1 × MAT-2 and ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ exhibited similar tolerance to cell wall stress (CR), and were more tolerant than Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE (Figure S4B). Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE showed a higher tolerance to NaCl (osmotic stress) than MAT-1 × MAT-2 , which in turn was more tolerant than ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ (Figure S4B). In addition, there was no significant difference in tolerance to sorbitol between the wild type and mutants under dikaryotic hyphae growth conditions (Figure S4B).

S . cerevisiae TPO1 has been reported to mediate tolerance to oxidative stress (Krüger et al. 2013 ). We then evaluated the sporidia growth of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE strains under exposure to H 2 O 2 of various concentrations. No significant difference in sensitivity to low concentrations of H 2 O 2 (0.2 or 0.5 mmol/L) between MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE ( Figure 3A ). However, ss1tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE strains were more sensitive than MAT-1 to high concentrations of H 2 O 2 (1 mmol/L; Figure 3A ). On the other hand, a low concentration of H 2 O 2 (0.2 mmol/L) slightly promoted the growth of dikaryotic hyphae in MAT-1 × MAT-2 , and H 2 O 2 (0.5 mmol/L) slightly inhibited the hyphal growth of all strains ( Figure 3B ). Under high H 2 O 2 concentrations (1 mmol/L), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE did not produce dikaryotic hyphae, whereas MAT-1 × MAT-2 produced extremely short hyphae ( Figure 3B ). We concluded that ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE were more sensitive to oxidative stress than MAT-1 × MAT-2 . We then measured the intracellular H 2 O 2 content of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE , but found no significant differences among the three strains ( Figure 3C ). We were curious about the effect of antioxidants on dikaryotic hyphal growth, especially in mutants that are hypersensitive to oxidative stress compared to wild type. Exogenous addition of the antioxidants glutathione (GSH), vitamin C, or N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) slightly suppressed hyphal growth of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and inhibited Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE hyphae growth ( Figure 3D ).

SsTPO1 participates in resistance to oxidative stress and host ROS accumulation. (A) Growth of haploid cells on PDA containing H 2 O 2 (0.2 mmol/L, 0.5 mmol/L, or 1 mmol/L) or without H 2 O 2 (served as a control), assessed at 2–3 d post cultivation. (B) Growth of dikaryotic hyphae of MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE grown on PDA medium supplemented with or without (control) H 2 O 2 . Scale bar = 1 mm. (C) Measurement of intracellular H 2 O 2 level of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE strains. Bar chart depicts the mean ± S.E. derived from three independent biological repeats, each containing four replications, ns represents no significance. (D) Mating assay under treatment of antioxidants. GSH, NAC, or VC was respectively supplemented to reach the final concentration of 1 mmol/L; PDA without treatment served as a control. MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). Scale bar = 1 mm. (E) Visualization of ROS accumulation by DAB staining. PUT, SPD, or SPM was added in mixed sporidia to reach the final concentration of 0.1 mmol/L or 1 mmol/L, and untreated sporidia served as controls. MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). Scale bar = 100 μm.

Our previous study revealed that in the early stage of WT infection (48–96 hpi), PUT promoted host ROS accumulation, whereas SPD suppressed host ROS accumulation (Yin et al. 2024b ). Therefore, we further investigated whether SsTPO1-mediated polyamine transport affected ROS accumulation in sugarcane tissues infected by S. scitamineum using DAB staining at 48 and 96 hpi. The results showed that the ROS levels in sugarcane inoculated with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE were higher than those in sugarcane inoculated with MAT-1 × MAT-2 in the early stage of infection ( Figure 3E ). However, the exogenous addition of PUT or SPD did not affect ROS accumulation in sugarcane tissues infected with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( Figure 3E ). RT-qPCR analysis showed that the relative expression levels of ROS-related genes, CAT1 , POD , and RBOH (respiratory burst oxidase) were significantly lower at 96 hpi than at 48 hpi following MAT-1 × MAT-2 infection (Figure S4C). However, the relative expression levels of CAT1 , POD , and RBOH were significantly lower at 48 and 96 hpi following infection with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE compared to MAT-1 × MAT-2 at 48 hpi (Figure S4C).

In summary, we conclude that SsTPO1-mediated polyamine transport regulates the resistance of fungal cells to oxidative stress as well as host plant ROS accumulation during S. scitamineum infection.

The polyamine transport capacity of yeast TPO1 is influenced by pH, with alkaline pH catalysing polyamine uptake and acidic pH facilitating polyamine extrusion (Uemura et al. 2005 ; Sampathkumar and Drouin 2015 ). We then investigated the individual and combined effects of four factors: SsTPO1, pH, polyamines (PUT, SPD, SPM), and H 2 O 2 , on the growth of sporidia and dikaryotic hyphae in S. scitamineum . Under neutral pH conditions (PDA medium, pH = 6.5), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ demonstrated more robust dikaryotic hyphae than MAT-1 × MAT-2 , which in turn was stronger than Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( Figure 4 ). Under alkaline conditions (pH = 10), hyphal growth of MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE was suppressed. However, ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ still exhibited stronger growth than the wild type and overexpression strains ( Figure 4 ). Under acidic conditions (pH = 5), the hyphal growth of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE was completely inhibited, whereas MAT-1 × MAT-2 still managed to grow some dikaryotic hyphae ( Figure 4 ). These results suggest that SsTPO1-based regulation of hyphal growth is dependent on environmental pH conditions. Both PUT and SPD were able to partially restore hyphal growth under acidic conditions for MAT-1 × MAT-2 and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE and to fully restore hyphal growth of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ under acidic conditions, with SPD being more effective than PUT ( Figure 4 ). In contrast, only SPD partially restored dikaryotic hyphae under alkaline conditions ( Figure 4 ). Moreover, treatment with polyamines did not affect sporidia growth under neutral, acidic, or alkaline conditions, with the ss1tpo1 Δ mutant showing stronger growth than MAT-1 and Ss1TPO1-OE strains (Figure S5A).

pH mediates SsTPO1-regulation of sexual mating/filamentation under oxidative stress. Mating assays were performed under neutral (pH = 6.5), acidic (pH = 5), or alkaline (pH = 10) conditions, containing or without (control) supplement of PUT (5 mmol/L), SPD (5 mmol/L), SPM (2 mmol/L), or H 2 O 2 (0.8 mmol/L). MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). Scale bar = 1 mm.

In contrast, H 2 O 2 (0.8 mmol/L) suppressed hyphal growth of MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE under neutral pH conditions, but slightly promoted hyphal growth of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ under both acidic and alkaline conditions ( Figure 4 ). Moreover, the sporidia growth of ss1tpo1 Δ mutant under neutral and alkaline conditions was stronger than that of MAT-1 , which was in turn stronger than that of Ss1TPO1-OE strain under oxidative stress treatment (0.8 mmol/L H 2 O 2 ; Figure S5A). Under acidic conditions, the growth of all three strains was comparable (Figure S5A). In particular, under oxidative stress combined with alkaline conditions, S. scitamineum growth was optimal (Figure S5A).

These results demonstrate that environmental pH modulated SsTPO1 function in polyamine transport, thereby regulating S. scitamineum hyphae growth under oxidative stress conditions.

The genes involved in the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway, SsGPA3 , SsUAC1 , and SsADR1 , were significantly down-regulated in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE , whereas SsPRF1 was significantly upregulated by more than 20-folds in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( Figure 1E ). Therefore, we investigated whether SsTPO1 affects the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway. First, the addition of cAMP (0.1 or 1 mmol/L) did not affect the sporidia growth of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, or Ss1TPO1-OE strains (Figure S5B). However, low concentrations (0.1 mmol/L) of cAMP slightly promoted hyphal growth in MAT-1 × MAT-2 and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE . In contrast, a high concentration (1 mmol/L) of cAMP inhibited hyphal growth in all tested strains ( Figure 5A ). Next, we measured intracellular cAMP levels in the sporidia and dikaryotic hyphae. Intracellular cAMP levels were significantly increased in ss1tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE sporidia compared to MAT-1 ( p < 0.05) as well as under sexual mating/filamentous growth condition ( p < 0.05 and 0.01, respectively) ( Figure 5B ).

SsTPO1 interacts with cAMP-PKA signaling and autophagy. (A) Mating assay under cAMP supplement. PDA medium without exogenous cAMP served as a control. MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). Scale bar = 1 mm. (B) Measurement of intracellular cAMP levels of haploid MAT-1 , ss1tpo Δ or Ss1TPO1-OE cells, or under mating condition MAT-1 × MAT-2 , ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE . (C) SsTPO1 positively regulates autophagy. Full-length or PE-conjugated form of SsAtg8 were detected using anti-ATG8 antibody, the ratio of ATG8-PE/ATG8 was calculated based on pixel intensity of the detected bands. *: Non-specific bands. Coomassie brilliant blue (CBB) staining served as loading control. (D) Mating assay under treatment of autophagy inducer rapamycin (RAPA; 55 nmol/L). Undertreated cultures served as control. MAT-1 × MAT-2 (WT), ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ ( sstpo1 Δ), Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( SsTPO1-OE ). Scale bar = 1 mm. (E) Visualization of mCherry-SsTPO1 and GFP-SsATG8 in haploid sporidia, under autophagy non-inducing (YePS) or inducing (MM-N) conditions. Arrows: mCherry-SsTPO1 signals on vesicles partially overlapped with GFP-Atg8. Arrowheads: mCherry-SsTPO1 signals inside vacuolar lumen. Scale bar = 10 μm. (F) Visualization of mCherry-SsTPO1 in MAT-1 and ss1atg8 Δ mutant, under autophagy non-inducing (YePS) or inducing (MM-N) conditions. Arrows: mCherry-SsTPO1 signals on membrane; arrowheads: mCherry-SsTPO1 signals inside vacuolar lumen. Scale bar = 10 μm. For bar charts in (B), mean ± S.E. was derived from three independent biological repeats, each containing three replications. *, p < 0.05, **, p < 0.01, ns represents no significance.

In conclusion, we propose that SsTPO1 affects the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway to control hyphal growth in S. scitamineum .

We evaluated the autophagic activity of MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE strains by detecting the full-length SsAtg8 peptide (15 kDa) and the PE-conjugated variant SsAtg8-PE (slightly lower than 15 kDa) following an established method (Kabeya et al. 2000 ). When cultured in YePS medium (nutrient-rich), MAT-1 cells exhibited low levels of SsAtg8-PE ( Figure 5C ), indicating that autophagy was suppressed under these conditions. When grown in MM-N medium (nitrogen starvation), MAT-1 cells showed increased SsAtg8-PE levels ( Figure 5C ), reflecting autophagy induction. Levels of SsAtg8-PE accumulation were significantly increased in Ss1TPO1-OE strain cultivated in either YePS or MM-N medium ( Figure 5C ), indicating that SsTPO1 positively regulates autophagy.

Furthermore, we examined the relative expression levels of autophagy genes in MAT-1 , ss1tpo1 Δ, and Ss1TPO1-OE strains. RT-qPCR analysis revealed that after 4 h of induction in MM-N medium, SsATG1 and SsATG13 were up-regulated, whereas SsATG8 was down-regulated in Ss1TPO1-OE compared to MAT-1 (Figure S5C). Moreover, exogenous addition of the established autophagy inducer, rapamycin (Yoo et al. 2019 ) (55 nmol/L), slightly promoted hyphal growth in ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ, but mildly inhibited hyphal growth in MAT-1 × MAT2 and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE ( Figure 5D ).

Next, we created the GFP-SsATG8:Ss1TPO1-OE strain and used this strain to observe autophagic flux in Ss1TPO1-OE strain in comparison with the wild type ( MAT-1 ). Fluorescence microscopy showed that the mCherry-SsTPO1 signals were partially overlapped with GFP-SsATG8 on small punctates likely corresponding to autophagic vesicles, when grown in YePS medium ( Figure 5E , arrows). Upon nitrogen starvation, the mCherry-SsTPO1 signal appeared inside the lumen of large vacuoles together with GFP-ATG8 ( Figure 5E , arrowheads). The Ss1TPO1-OE strain was generated by tagging the SsTPO1 protein with an mCherry protein at its N-terminus, creating the fusion protein mCherry-SsTPO1. We also created the mCherry-SsTPO1:ss1atg8 Δ strain. The subcellular localisation of SsTPO1 was then observed and compared in wild-type and autophagy deficient conditions, by using fluorescence microscopy. Under nutrient-rich conditions, the majority of the mCherry-SsTPO1 signals were localised on the membrane ( Figure 5F , arrows). In contrast, while the predominant mCherry-SsTPO1 signal was observed within the vacuolar lumen under nitrogen starvation ( Figure 5F , arrowheads). On the other hand, in the atg8 Δ background, the majority of the mCherry-SsTPO1 signals were localised on the membrane under nutrient-rich conditions ( Figure 5F , arrows). In contrast, under nitrogen starvation, while the predominant mCherry-SsTPO1 signal remained on the membrane ( Figure 5F , arrows), a smaller proportion was observed within the vacuolar lumen ( Figure 5F , arrowheads). Therefore, we hypothesised that autophagy facilitates the engulfment of SsTPO1 from the membrane to the lumen of the vacuole, likely for degradation, and thus modulates polyamine transport in S. scitamineum .

In summary, our results demonstrate that S. scitamineum SsTPO1 positively regulates autophagy and may depend on autophagy for turnover.
sections.discussion:
MFS proteins are responsible for transporting various metabolite compounds (Del Sorbo et al. 2000 ; Saier and Paulsen 2001 ; Yen et al. 2010 ), which involved in growth, development, pathogenicity, and interactions with host plants in pathogenic fungi. In Colletotrichum gloeosporioides , CgMFS1 plays a crucial role in sugar transport, oxidative stress responses, and pathogenicity (Liu et al. 2021 ). FgMFS1 is a salicylic acid (SA) efflux pump critical for the response to SA in host wheat, thus regulating the pathogenicity of F. graminearum (Chen et al. 2021 ). In addition, MFS transporters have been implicated in the resistance mechanisms against the fungal toxin deoxynivalenol (DON) in F. graminearum (Wang et al. 2018 ). Botrytis cinerea BcmfsG is involved in the efflux of glucosinolate breakdown products during fungus-plant interactions (Vela-Corcía et al. 2019 ) and BcSDR1 is a key regulator of growth, development, and pathogenicity by serving as a transmembrane transporter of glucose (Zang et al. 2018 ; Si et al. 2022 ).

S . cerevisiae TPO1-TPO5 transporters belong to MSF and are capable of transporting polyamines (Albertsen et al. 2003 ). TPO1, TPO2, TPO3, and TPO4 are localised on the plasma and vacuolar membranes (Uemura et al. 2005 ). Notably, TPO1 facilitates polyamine uptake at alkaline pH and polyamine efflux at acidic pH (Uemura et al. 2005 ; Sampathkumar and Drouin 2015 ). In this study, we identified a candidate TPO1 transporter in S. scitamineum and named it SsTPO1. The mCherry-SsTPO1 fusion protein was localised on the membrane of intracellular compartments, likely vacuoles ( Figure 5G ), consistent with its yeast ortholog. Characterisation of the deletion or overexpression mutant of SsTPO1 ( Figure 1A–C ) confirmed that it is likely responsible for the uptake of PUT, and efflux of SPD and SPM, under neutral pH.

The sstpo1 Δ mutant displayed enhanced hyphal growth ( Figures 1D , S3E), likely because of decreased PUT levels and/or increased SPD levels within the cell. However, hyphal growth was completely abolished in both ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE under acidic pH conditions, but partially reduced under alkaline conditions ( Figure 4 ). We infer that SsTPO1-mediated polyamine transport and the consequent regulation of hyphae growth are likely dependent on pH. This is consistent with what has been reported in S. cerevisiae , as TPO1 is a polyamine-H + antiporter with a pH-dependent transport function.

SPD and SPM are capable of scavenging free radicals (Lovaas and Carlin 1991 ) and consuming H 2 O 2 (Krüger et al. 2013 ), therefore they can act as antioxidants to modulate the intracellular redox state. In S. cerevisiae , TPO1 regulates SPD and SPM levels in response to oxidative stress, and affects the transcriptional levels of genes encoding antioxidant proteins (Krüger et al. 2013 ). In this study, we observed that hyphal growth of ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ and Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE was hypersensitive to oxidative stress compared to MAT-1 × MAT-2 ( Figure 3B ), indicating that intracellular polyamine balance contributes to tolerance to oxidative stress. Such polyamine-based oxidative stress tolerance may be essential for fungal pathogenicity, as disease symptoms were weakened or completely lost in sugarcane plants infected with ss1tpo1 Δ × ss2tpo1 Δ or Ss1TPO1-OE × Ss2TPO1-OE mutants ( Figure 2A,B ). Therefore, either its absence or overexpression leads to disturbance of intracellular polyamines levels, which are important for S. scitamineum pathogenicity.

Consistent with our previous work, we found that polyamine homeostasis interacts with the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway that controls S. scitaminem sexual mating/filamentation (Yin et al. 2024a , 2024b ). We found that intracellular levels of cAMP were disrupted in the SsTPO1 mutants ( Figure 5B ). We further found that autophagy induction was suppressed in the deletion mutant of Ss1TPO1 , whereas it was enhanced in the mutant overexpressing Ss1TPO1 ( Figure 5C ), demonstrating that SsTPO1 positively regulates autophagy. We also observed that the subcellular localisation of mCherry-SsTPO1 changed from the membrane to the lumen of vacuoles upon autophagy induction ( Figure 5E,F ). We hypothesised that autophagy may facilitate the turnover of SsTPO1 and thus contribute to intracellular polyamine homeostasis in S. scitamineum .

In summary, SsTPO1 plays a role in the transport of polyamines (PUT, SPD, and SPM), thereby maintaining intracellular polyamine homeostasis in S. scitamineum . SsTPO1-mediated polyamine transport contributes to modulation of the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway, oxidative stress response, and autophagy induction, which in turn affect dikaryotic hyphae formation and invasive growth during host infection. The working model is shown in Figure 6 .

A proposed working model. SsTPO1 maintains intracellular polyamines homeostasis likely by pumping in PUT and/or pumping out SPD/SPM. PUT and SPD are capable of affecting intracellular ROS levels and autophagy activity, thereby regulating sexual mating/filamentation and pathogenicity of Sporisorium scitamineum .
